overview: Imagine a map so huge that it stretches from the lower Ob River to Chukotka, yet gives every community inside one label: “Siberians.” Between 1279 and 1530, no single nation, ruler or language joined this enormous space. Khanty and Mansi river principalities, Samoyedic-speaking tundra communities, Yeniseian and Tungusic groups, Sakha newcomers on the Lena, and peoples of Kamchatka and Chukotka followed different histories. Some fished great rivers; some hunted forest animals or sea mammals; some herded reindeer, cattle or horses. Mongol and later khanate networks demanded tribute, moved captives and carried northern furs into long-distance trade. Archaeology finds wooden settlements, birchbark, fur clothing, metal imports, parasites from fish and a few striking burials. Those finds are vivid but local: one child's grave cannot describe a continent. The atlas shape is best read as leftover map space around the Golden Horde, Yuan, Sibir and Oirat polygons. Its 1530 disappearance is another redraw, not the end of Indigenous Siberian peoples, whose communities and languages continued.

periods.title: 1279 snapshot: an imperial-edge umbrella appears
periods.summary: The first exact feature wraps the northern and eastern spaces left outside Golden Horde and Yuan polygons. Mongol governments nevertheless maintained political, economic and administrative relations with forest peoples, so the blank-looking north was connected rather than isolated.

periods.title: 1300 snapshot: the outline freezes while societies move
periods.summary: The 1300 geometry is coordinate-for-coordinate identical to 1279 for a full century. Local communities, migrations, exchange and ecological cycles did not freeze with it. The repeated polygon records basemap reuse, not stable borders or a century-long united government.

periods.title: 1400 snapshot: Horde fragmentation and regional change
periods.summary: The atlas keeps nearly the same northern umbrella while relabeling much of western Siberia White Horde and retaining a Yuan polygon after the Yuan court lost China. In real politics, Golden Horde unity fractured and regional successor states, including Sibir, formed during the fifteenth century.

periods.title: 1492 snapshot: the west is cut away
periods.summary: The feature loses its far-western portion and begins near 54 degrees east. Atlas polygons assign tested southern and western points to Sibir, Oirat and Chagatai labels, while the umbrella still covers the Lena, Kolyma, Okhotsk, Kamchatka and Chukotka. This is cartographic partition, not ethnic sorting.

periods.title: 1500 snapshot: one last contraction before fragmentation
periods.summary: The western bound jumps east to about 65 degrees and the geometry becomes one polygon. The atlas prematurely places Salekhard under Moscow. At 1530 the umbrella vanishes into a few named groups, empires and vast unassigned gaps, without evidence of one conquest or common ending.

sections.title: Audit the umbrella and its exact geometry

items.text: The indexed object is exactly id “siberians,” label “Siberians,” kind “culture,” circa 1279 to 1530, generated from historical basemaps. It has five border intervals, no existing card and no override. Its imported summary instead defines modern ethnic Russians in Siberia, an anachronism that this packet rejects rather than polishing.

At 1279 and 1300 the feature is the same MultiPolygon: two parts, two rings and 1,050 positions, bounded by 43.703° to 180° east and 50.957° to 77.592° north. Both coordinate arrays hash to 0e8406ba3470084247f42b4d081bfd074d5877aef63dfb94c7fa4a581fdfc1f5. Geometry identity proves reuse, not sovereignty.

The 1400 feature still has two parts, two rings and 1,050 positions, with minute coordinate changes and hash ee0eb8794be0252e8520dd5020e1eaff49db1b02c628b59d6131f1d9c43fd5fd. Tested lower Ob, Nadym, Yenisei, upper and middle Lena, Kolyma, Okhotsk, Kamchatka and Chukotka points remain inside, while southern Siberia remains outside.

At 1492 the umbrella contracts to 985 positions and a western bound near 54.017° east; its hash is fe7c74871fbe24aa929e14581b44058cafd22f346ba99f92f9185cff26f650a2. At 1500 it becomes one polygon with 810 positions, begins near 65.062° east and hashes to 6f937a9355db8f34fc1b97ed893a444a288546665de09802bde8fe91b2853a77. The shrinking west edge is measurable.

The id is absent at 1100 and 1200, when generic labels divide the same broad zone among Finno-Ugric taiga communities, Paleo-Siberian communities, Tungusic groups, Arctic marine hunters and Mongol power. It is absent again at 1530. Those seams change the map's vocabulary; they do not create or dissolve real peoples overnight.

sections.title: Meet many regions, languages and peoples

items.text: Central and western Siberia contained speakers of Uralic languages, including Ugric Khanty and Mansi and Samoyedic Nenets, Enets, Nganasan and Selkup, alongside Yeniseian, Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic languages. Contact could reshape grammar and vocabulary. A language family is not a medieval state, and multilingual neighbors were not interchangeable.

Farther east, Chukotko-Kamchatkan languages, Yukaghir, Nivkh and Ket belong to different families or isolates. The older umbrella term “Palaeoasiatic” grouped them geographically rather than proving one ancestry or culture. It is useful for spotting diversity and dangerous when treated as a single people-name.

Tundra, boreal forest, great river basins and Pacific coasts offered different seasonal opportunities. Smithsonian materials distinguish Nenets, Khanty, Evenk and Chukchi and describe fisheries, land animals and marine mammals across contrasting habitats. The card therefore says “some communities,” never “the Siberians always,” when describing subsistence.

The historical record is uneven by region. Archaeology, neighboring courts' texts and much later oral or ethnographic collections illuminate different pieces. The official Siberian archaeology museum itself organizes many archaeological periods and traditions, including early states, nomadic sites, Khanty, Mansi, Selkup and Amur religious material, rather than one continuous national exhibit.

The imported “Siberiaks” summary describes an ethnographic subgroup of Russians, a category formed after eastward Russian settlement. That cannot define people living from the Ob to the Pacific in 1279. The medieval card preserves the exact database id only as a display key and repeatedly calls its subject an atlas umbrella.

sections.title: Trace political networks without inventing one state

items.text: Mongol power did reach forest peoples through political, administrative and economic relationships, while northern goods entered east-west trade. Rule could mean tribute, envoys, military demands or alliance rather than dense occupation of every river valley. The atlas leaves much of the north outside Golden Horde and Yuan polygons, but outside a polygon did not mean outside history.

Medieval Russian sources describe Yugra, the Khanty and Mansi world near the Ob and Urals, as several principalities. Princes gathered retinues and allies; wooden stockades at river bends or mouths housed a prince, family, servants, stores and warriors. This localized hierarchy is concrete evidence against a continent-wide “Siberian” government.

After Toqtamish's death and Edigu's struggles, Golden Horde political unity fractured. Regional yurts became foundations for fifteenth-century successor states including the Siberian Khanate. Sibir belonged to the southwestern forest-steppe, however; it did not rule all the territory the atlas colors “Siberians,” especially Kamchatka or Chukotka.

The 1492 snapshot itself keeps Sibir separate: Surgut, Tyumen, Tobolsk and Khanty-Mansiysk test inside “khanate-of-sibir,” while the target retains northern and eastern points. Narym, Tomsk and Krasnoyarsk test as Oirat, and southern Baikal and Amur points as Chagatai. These imported labels are broad too, but they disprove aliasing Sibir with “Siberians.”

In the far east, relations with Yuan and Ming courts affected selected Amur, Sakhalin and forest communities, while other groups remained politically organized at village, kin or regional-network scales. No consulted source supplies a ruler list, capital, law code or tax system shared from the lower Ob to the Bering Strait. The silence is meaningful, not a gap to fill imaginatively.

sections.title: Follow trade, tribute, captivity and conflict

items.text: Furs were major medieval luxury goods. Northwestern Siberia and northeastern Europe supplied exceptionally valued winter pelts to markets far away. Trapping therefore connected a hunter on a forest river with merchants and elites he might never meet, but demand could also sharpen tribute pressure and competition over routes.

A child burial on the Gydan Peninsula contained a bronze bowl probably made in eastern Iran or Central Asia, plus a metal knife haft, scabbard and silver earring. The burial predates the atlas interval, around 900 to 1100, yet it proves northern exchange networks existed before 1279. One grave cannot reveal the trader's whole route.

Mongol conquest and government moved people as well as goods. Captives could be distributed, sold or placed in different kinds of dependency, and some later gained mobility or manumission. This empire-wide pattern must be labeled context: it does not tell us how many northern people were seized or make every dependent worker a chattel slave.

The fourteenth- or fifteenth-century Atlasovskoye burial in Yakutia preserves lethal cutting injuries and unusually heavy physical stress in a young adult. Researchers consider alternatives including warrior or enslaved status, with other features possibly indicating high rank. That uncertainty is the honest result: trauma proves violence, not the person's job title.

Conflict also took place among local princes, retinues and neighboring powers, but heroic poetry collected centuries later cannot be read as a battle report. Khanty epics preserve a world of heroes, warfare, spirits and skilled work; historians compare them with archaeology and written records while keeping performance, collection date and remembered past distinct.

sections.title: Adapt to rivers, forests, tundra and coasts

items.text: There was no single Siberian economy. River communities could combine fishing and hunting; tundra groups moved with animals and seasons; southern forest-steppe people herded livestock; Pacific and Arctic coastal peoples took fish and marine mammals. Climate made planning essential, but local knowledge, tools and social cooperation mattered as much as toughness.

Reindeer use also varied. Research at Ust-Polui argues for domestic transport reindeer and helps trace the later rise of large-scale pastoralism in northwestern Siberia. It does not license a picture of every medieval family owning a vast herd. Reindeer hunting, transport and pastoral management had separate regional histories.

A twelfth- to thirteenth-century infant at Zeleniy Yar carried fish-parasite eggs, and the site held abundant fish remains. The result shows minimally cooked fish entered one very young child's diet near the lower Ob. It is startlingly personal evidence, but it does not establish every family's menu across the later atlas polygon.

Nadymskiy Gorodok, on an elevated island in the Nadym delta, preserves a long sequence of timber construction in the forest-tundra. Dendrochronology can date building and repair episodes and reveal how wood was selected. The settlement shows skilled architecture in one subarctic center, not a standard house plan for all northern Asia.

Arctic technologies traveled and changed through contact. Museum research tracks northern innovations alongside metallurgy, animal domestication and other technologies moving from different directions. Exchange was selective: receiving a metal vessel did not erase local woodworking, skin sewing or food knowledge, and an imported object does not identify its owner's language.

sections.title: See families, children and unequal social roles

items.text: A Yugra prince's fort could include his family, servants, warriors and separate storage buildings. Families outside the fort belonged to a wider principality, but surviving descriptions emphasize leaders more than ordinary households. Social rank was real; the evidence does not give household size, marriage age or an inheritance rule shared by all Khanty and Mansi communities.

Rich medieval child burials at Zeleny Yar include a hatchet, scabbards, bracelets and temple rings. Researchers cautiously discuss high status, showing that age did not erase social distinction. Grave goods express burial choices by survivors, however; they do not prove that the children used every object daily or reveal how most children were raised.

The Parisento burial held a child only about one to three years old with imported and locally familiar metal objects. Its disturbed state and missing skeleton sharply limit interpretation. It can show that families marked a child's death and participated in far-reaching material networks, not that every Arctic child possessed costly goods.

The Atlasovskoye adult's body combined possible high-status treatment with evidence of punishing labor and violent death. Researchers offer warrior and enslaved-person models rather than one certain answer. That tension reminds us that rank, coercion and work could intersect, and that a spectacular burial may belong to someone far from an average household.

Later Smithsonian records show that sleeping, seating and co-residence could express kinship, marriage, age, gender and status in northeastern Siberian homes. These comparisons help historians ask better questions, but they are not medieval census sheets. The card therefore avoids assigning one fixed women's role, men's role or family shape to the entire umbrella.

sections.title: Learn through speech, practice, memory and objects

items.text: Children likely learned the skills their households needed by listening, watching and practicing, yet no consulted medieval source gives a daily lesson schedule. Fishing, sewing, travel, animal knowledge and ritual competence all require teaching. This is a cautious inference from complex work, not evidence for one continent-wide school system or a universal age of apprenticeship.

Ket and Evenki oral histories and material traditions preserve collective memory, while scholars debate how directly later accounts connect to archaeological populations. Oral knowledge is evidence, not “nothing because it was not written.” It must still be dated, localized and compared with artifacts rather than copied backward as a word-for-word transcript from 1400.

Khanty heroic epics were recorded and edited in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Their seasons, geography, spirits, warfare and handiwork reveal an Indigenous intellectual world and the discipline of skilled performers. They are priceless continuity evidence, but their printed wording is later than 1279 to 1530 and cannot serve as an in-period manuscript sample.

This card gives no fake “Siberian” written-language sample. “Siberians” was not a language, and no securely dated 1279 to 1530 text authored in a language of the atlas umbrella was found in the consulted corpus. Arabic-script Sibir documents or Mongolian and Chinese imperial texts would represent adjacent courts, not everyone inside this residual polygon.

Script-bearing imported objects do not prove that their owners read the inscription. Research on adjacent northern forest regions shows alphabetic writing could arrive with traders, tribute takers and goods before local written cultures formed. Accordingly, the sample field is explicitly “none securely attributable”; original script, transliteration and translation are inapplicable rather than missing by accident.

sections.title: Eat, dress, shelter, work and sometimes play

items.text: Lower Ob evidence makes fish one secure local food. The Zeleniy Yar infant's parasite infection indicates raw or minimally cooked fish, while fish bones were abundant at the site. Cooking, freezing and drying practices varied, and the parasite also shows a cost of food choices. It is evidence for one region, not an all-Siberian recipe.

Zeleny Yar children's burials preserve fur coverings, worked leather, birchbark, metal ornaments and carefully built wooden or boat-shaped containers. These materials reveal skilled cutting, sewing and construction. They do not prove a universal outfit, and grave dress should not be turned into ordinary work clothes or a medieval fashion season.

Northeastern Siberian communities later used varied homes: portable skin tents, wooden houses and earth- or sod-covered dwellings, often shifting residence with seasonal fishing or hunting. Smithsonian evidence explains the engineering logic and social meaning. Because most examples are later, this card presents them as comparisons, not identical plans for a 1400 Kamchatkan house.

Nadym's wooden settlement required felling, transporting, shaping and repeatedly repairing timber in a treeless-edge environment. Those tasks imply cooperation and specialist judgment. Archaeology can reconstruct construction phases much better than bedtime routines, jokes or arguments inside the buildings, so the people remain more than a list of logs while the missing details stay missing.

No reliable target-period source in this packet names a children's game, toy rule or ordinary music session shared across the umbrella. People surely rested, told stories and amused one another, but “surely” is not a catalog entry. Later museum collections contain performance and play objects; they invite questions without becoming medieval proof.

sections.title: Face illness, water, waste and sanitation honestly

items.text: Parasite eggs from a Zeleniy Yar infant reveal infection linked to undercooked fish. That is medical evidence about disease exposure, not a surviving diagnosis or remedy. No consulted source records who cared for this child, what treatment was tried or how illness was explained. A parasite under a microscope cannot write the missing bedside story.

Fourteenth- and fifteenth-century soil at Nadym Gorodok also contained fish-related parasite evidence. Researchers use such remains to study diet, movement and health risks. The samples came from occupation layers, so the card does not rename them a toilet. Parasite eggs can reveal exposure while leaving disposal practices and treatment unknown.

The Atlasovskoye skeleton preserves severe workload-related pathology and fatal wounds. Bones can show stress, trauma and sometimes healing, but they rarely reveal the spoken name of a healer, an herbal recipe or whether care was effective. Later Siberian healing traditions exist; projecting them unchanged into this one fourteenth-century life would be careless.

The target polygon spans the Ob, Yenisei, Lena, Kolyma and many coastal drainages, while point tests follow no single watershed. Rivers supported travel and food in documented local cases, but a basemap cannot show how drinking water was fetched, stored, melted, boiled or kept apart from waste. No uniform water-treatment rule survives for the vast region.

No consulted authoritative target-period source securely identifies an ordinary household toilet, latrine, sewer, garbage-collection service or bathing rule for these diverse communities. Nadym's cultural layers offer parasite evidence, not a mapped sanitation system. The safest answer to “where was the toilet?” is regional evidence is too sparse to say.

sections.title: End the map label, preserve peoples and uncertainty

items.text: Frozen and furnished graves are not a random sample of society. Research on Yakut burials notes that burial in frozen ground was uncommon and surviving graves overrepresent certain places, dates and social positions. Archaeological visibility must not become a claim that elites, adult men or buried communities were the whole population.

Early Sakha burials and livestock evidence offer a localized picture of communities in the Lena region before Cossack conquest. They cannot stand for Khanty fishers, Nenets tundra communities or Chukchi coastal peoples. Their value is exactly their specificity: they replace a gray umbrella with one carefully dated regional story.

The 1530 redraw names Enets near Norilsk, Itelmen on Kamchatka and Chukchi near Anadyr, places a Komi polygon far into Nadym, assigns the Amur to Ming and leaves many tested central and eastern points blank. This is not a credible successor list. The override therefore supplies no predecessors, successors or fall date.

Russian conquest of Yakutia began only in the seventeenth century and brought new disease, foods, religion and colonial power. That history was devastating and transformative, but it comes after the atlas label ends. It cannot be moved backward to explain 1530, and conquest did not erase Sakha people or every earlier institution.

The ending is therefore “continuity” at the map seam, not victory, collapse or extinction. Political formations changed, people migrated and languages influenced one another. Khanty, Mansi, Nenets, Enets, Selkup, Ket, Evenk, Even, Sakha, Yukaghir, Nivkh, Chukchi, Koryak, Itelmen and other communities continued on their own historical paths beyond 1530.

ending.text: At 1530 the atlas removes its broad “Siberians” polygon and replaces only fragments with named peoples and neighboring states, while leaving much of central and eastern Siberia blank. No single war, dynasty or cultural ending explains that seam. Regional polities changed and later Russian conquest caused enormous disruption, but the diverse Indigenous communities, languages, skills and oral traditions continued. This is the end of a map bucket, not the end of peoples.
